title: Verification of KCL and KVL using LTspice
objective: Verify signed current and voltage balances in the assigned circuit.
prerequisite: Ohm’s law; reference directions; voltage polarity.
prelab: Mark a reference node, current arrows and voltage polarities before writing equations.
Write one node equation and one independent loop equation for the assigned circuit.
Predict what a negative current reading would mean.
observe: Use the assigned component values and the same reference directions in the calculation and simulation.
Measure the required branch currents and voltage drops at the operating point.
Calculate a signed KCL residual and a signed KVL residual; include units.
record: Branch current and reference arrow (A or mA)
postlab: Compare calculated and simulated values. Does rounding explain the residual?
Explain a negative reading using the chosen reference direction.
If a balance fails, identify one connection or sign convention to check first.
formula: Signed current and voltage sums must balance.

title: Node and mesh analysis using LTspice
objective: Solve the assigned network using node voltages and mesh currents, then compare with simulation.
prelab: Identify unknown node voltages and any voltage already fixed by a grounded source.
Choose mesh-current directions and write the shared-branch current with consistent signs.
Decide whether the assigned circuit needs a supernode or supermesh. Explain why.
observe: Solve the simultaneous equations before checking the simulator output.
Record node voltages relative to the same reference node.
Convert mesh currents into physical branch currents, then compare those branch currents with simulation.
record: Mesh current and direction (A or mA)
postlab: Do node and mesh methods predict the same physical branch currents?
Why can a mesh current differ from the current in a shared branch?
Which measurement would help locate an incorrect equation sign?

title: Superposition, Thevenin’s and Norton’s theorems using LTspice
objective: Validate source contributions and terminal-equivalent circuits under the same load.
prerequisite: Node or mesh analysis; source transformation.
prelab: Define the response quantity and the two load terminals.
Explain how each independent source is deactivated in an ideal circuit model.
Predict which quantities must agree between the original circuit and its equivalent.
observe: Record each independent-source contribution with its sign, then add voltage or current responses.
Find the open-circuit voltage and equivalent resistance seen from the load port.
Reconnect the same load to the original, Thevenin and Norton circuits and compare terminal quantities.
record: Individual and total response (V or A)
Thevenin voltage (V); equivalent resistance (Ω); Norton current (A)
Load voltage, load current and load resistance
postlab: Does the sum of source contributions match the full-circuit response?
Why must the load remain outside the equivalent-source boundary?
Explain why separate source powers generally cannot be added using superposition.
formula: The two equivalent forms use the same terminal resistance.

title: Transient analysis of RL and RC circuits
objective: Analyse initial values, final values and time constants of the assigned first-order circuits.
prerequisite: KVL/KCL; exponential response; capacitor and inductor state variables.
prelab: State the capacitor voltage or inductor current immediately before switching.
Predict the state immediately after switching and the eventual DC value.
Find the resistance seen by the storage element for the assigned source conditions.
observe: Choose a simulation interval and time resolution that show both the early response and settling trend.
Mark the theoretical time constant on the waveform.
Compare initial, one-time-constant and late-time values without assuming exact finite-time settling.
record: Time (s); capacitor voltage (V) or inductor current (A)
Initial and final state values; theoretical time constant (s)
State at one time constant; simulated time-constant estimate
postlab: Compare the time-constant estimate with the theoretical value.
Explain why a charging curve and a discharging curve use different absolute voltage readings at one time constant.
How could initial stored energy change the observed response?
formula: Use the resistance seen by the storage element for the stated switching condition.

title: Resonance analysis of RLC circuits using LTspice
objective: Examine resonance and frequency response with a clearly defined circuit topology and plotted quantity.
prerequisite: Complex impedance; frequency sweeps; RMS quantities.
prelab: State whether the assigned RLC circuit is series or parallel.
Name the quantity plotted in the frequency sweep and its units.
Predict whether source-current magnitude should rise or fall near resonance for the selected drive and topology.
observe: Sweep across a range that includes both sides of resonance.
Record the resonant frequency and the response magnitude there.
If finding bandwidth, state the response and drive condition used to define its half-power points.
record: Resonant frequency (Hz); peak or minimum response
postlab: Compare resonance with the ideal LC estimate and explain the assumptions.
Why is a source-current maximum not a universal definition of resonance?
Explain which measurement would justify a reported bandwidth or Q value.
formula: Ideal LC resonance estimate; state the topology and component model used.

title: AC circuit and phasor analysis using LTspice
objective: Compare RMS magnitudes, phase angles and phasor sums in the assigned AC network.
prelab: Choose one phase reference and label the current/voltage directions.
Predict whether the relevant current leads or lags the reference voltage.
Write the appropriate phasor KVL or KCL equation before adding magnitudes.
observe: Use the same frequency and RMS/peak convention in your calculation and simulation comparison.
Record voltage and current phase angles against the same reference.
Add rectangular phasor components and check the resulting magnitude and angle.
record: Voltage/current magnitudes (V, A) and phase angles (°)
Phasor sum and the reference directions used
postlab: Why can the sum of component-voltage magnitudes exceed the source magnitude?
Compare the phasor result with the time-domain lead/lag observation.
Explain how a reversed current reference changes the reported phase angle.

title: Measurement of RC and RL time constants
objective: Estimate time constants from measured charging or decay waveforms.
prelab: Predict initial and final values for the assigned switching condition.
Calculate the theoretical time constant, including relevant source or winding resistance.
Identify the waveform level corresponding to 63.2% of a rising change or 36.8% of a remaining decay.
observe: Use the instructor-approved circuit, instrument settings and supply limits.
Measure the waveform relative to its actual initial and final values.
Repeat the time-constant estimate and record relevant component tolerances or loading effects.
record: Measured resistance, capacitance or inductance, with units
Initial/final state values; selected threshold level
postlab: Compare measured and predicted time constants using a stated percentage difference.
How might probe loading, component tolerance or coil resistance affect the result?
Why is one fixed voltage threshold unsuitable for every charging/discharging case?

title: Resonance characteristics of an RLC circuit
objective: Measure resonance, bandwidth and quality factor for a defined response.
prerequisite: RLC frequency response; impedance; instrument measurement conventions.
prelab: Identify the circuit topology, source type and measured output.
Predict resonance using the stated component model.
Define how the relevant half-power boundaries will be identified from that output.
observe: Use the assigned circuit and approved instrument ranges.
Take enough points near resonance to locate the relevant peak or minimum.
Record boundary frequencies only when the selected measurement supports the stated bandwidth definition.
postlab: Compare measured resonance with the ideal estimate and discuss possible nonideal effects.
Explain how the chosen output and source determine the bandwidth measurement.
What is the effect of additional damping in your measured response?
formula: Apply these to the specified resonant response and its appropriate boundary frequencies.

title: PN junction diode, Zener diode and LED characteristics
objective: Measure and compare device characteristics within the approved operating ranges.
prerequisite: Diode polarity; current limiting; voltage/current measurement.
prelab: Identify each device and its terminal polarity from its datasheet or lab instructions.
Explain how ratings determine the allowed sweep range and current-limiting resistor.
Sketch the expected qualitative characteristic of each assigned device.
observe: Use the instructor-approved circuit and current limits for each device.
Record device voltage and current with signs and units.
Keep measurement conditions consistent when comparing characteristics.
record: Device type; polarity; approved operating range
postlab: How do the measured characteristics differ among the three devices?
Why is a single fixed forward-voltage approximation only a limited model?
Explain why the resistor and device ratings remain important near a characteristic knee.

title: BJT as a switch
objective: Relate base drive, collector current and collector-emitter voltage to switching state.
prerequisite: BJT terminals; cutoff and saturation; resistive load behaviour.
prelab: Identify the assigned transistor terminals and reference polarities.
Estimate the load current required in the on state.
Explain why active-region current gain alone does not guarantee saturation.
observe: Use the assigned base-drive and load circuit with approved supply/current limits.
Measure base current, collector current and collector-emitter voltage in each input state.
Use the measured quantities to identify cutoff or saturation.
postlab: What measured evidence supports your on/off state labels?
How does insufficient base drive alter the collector-emitter voltage and load response?
Compare the measured collector-to-base current ratio with the assumption used to design the drive.

title: MOSFET as a switch
objective: Relate gate-source drive, load current and drain-source voltage to switching behaviour.
prerequisite: MOSFET terminals; gate-source voltage; on-state resistance.
prelab: Identify the device terminals and channel type.
Distinguish threshold voltage from a gate drive at which on-state resistance is specified.
Predict the on-state current and conduction loss using the assigned load and stated device data.
observe: Use the instructor-approved gate-drive and load circuit.
Measure gate-source voltage, drain-source voltage and load current in each input state.
Compare the observed on-state behaviour with the device data at the actual gate drive.
record: On-state power estimate (W); stated device conditions
postlab: Why can a MOSFET conduct some current near threshold without being a good on-state switch?
Why must gate voltage be referenced to the source terminal?
Discuss differences between a resistive conduction-loss estimate and total switching loss.
formula: Use on-state resistance specified for the actual gate-drive and operating conditions.

title: SCR, DIAC and TRIAC characteristics
objective: Compare triggering, conduction polarity and holding behaviour of the assigned power devices.
prerequisite: Diode polarity; AC waveforms; switching states.
prelab: Sketch the expected qualitative characteristic and conduction polarity of each device.
Distinguish triggering, latching current and holding current where applicable.
Predict whether removing a gate signal alone will stop conduction in the assigned circuit.
observe: Use only the approved trainer, circuit and instrument settings under the lab instructor’s supervision.
Record the device, excitation conditions and measured voltages/currents for each observation.
Identify triggering and turn-off behaviour from the measured response rather than gate signal alone.
record: Device voltage (V); current (mA or A); trigger condition
Observed latching, holding or commutation behaviour
postlab: Compare the conduction directions and triggering mechanisms of the three devices.
Explain the difference between latching and holding behaviour for the observed device.
How can a current zero affect turn-off in the approved AC experiment?
